oil.summary: Crude prices sold off sharply on Tuesday as a US-Iran military pause extended into a fourth consecutive night, removing the geopolitical premium that had pushed Brent to $100 last week. WTI settled at $81.52 (-1.33%) and Brent at $86.59 (-2.00%), with RBOB gasoline bearing the steepest correction at -4.45%. Despite the diplomatic de-escalation, structural supply risks remain: Red Sea tanker traffic has hit a multi-month low on persistent Houthi threats, Saudi Arabia is reportedly weighing higher Asia-bound crude OSPs to offset elevated shipping costs, and Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil facilities and drone disruptions to Kazakh pipeline flows add tail risk to the supply picture. Iran claims it has met over 60% of its annual oil revenue target despite sanctions and war. The month-on-month gains — Brent +20%, Heating Oil +26% — underline how violently the conflict premium was priced in.
drivers: US-Iran military pause extends to four nights, triggering broad unwind of conflict premium
Houthi threat keeps Red Sea tanker traffic at multi-month lows; Saudi Arabia may raise Asia crude OSPs
Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil facilities and drone disruption to Kazakh flows provide residual supply-side risk

gas.summary: Henry Hub continued to weaken, falling 2.49% to $2.697/MMBtu and now down 16.5% over the past month, suggesting ample domestic supply conditions in the US. TTF was more resilient, slipping just 0.78% to €57.8/MWh, though the contract remains up a sharp 41.7% on the month — a reflection of the broader Middle East supply anxiety that has gripped European gas markets. On the supply-development side, Eni and TotalEnergies took a final investment decision on the Cronos gas field offshore Cyprus, marking the eastern Mediterranean country's first deepwater gas project. Separately, escalating anti-government protests in Libya — triggered by power cuts and high electricity bills — have spread to the Mellitah oil and gas complex, threatening near-term Libyan supply. News flow for this sector is relatively thin today beyond these three items.
drivers: Henry Hub slides further (-2.49% 1d, -16.5% 1m), reflecting loose US domestic supply fundamentals
Eni/TotalEnergies reach FID on Cyprus Cronos deepwater gas field, adding long-term eastern Med supply
Libyan protesters enter the Mellitah oil and gas complex, raising near-term North African supply disruption risk

power.summary: EU carbon allowances (EUA) edged down 0.45% to $77.63, broadly stable on the week (-1.24%) and modestly positive on the month (+3.71%), offering little directional signal amid competing forces. The most significant power-sector headline was a drone attack on a UAE nuclear power plant — reported to have briefly lifted oil prices to a two-week high — underscoring how conflict-related infrastructure risk is now extending beyond hydrocarbons to nuclear assets. On the demand-side of the nuclear story, Tata Power has announced plans to commission India's first privately owned nuclear plant by 2032, following India's opening of the civil nuclear sector to private capital. Libyan protests spilling into energy infrastructure are a reminder that power supply insecurity is driving unrest across the region. Trump's mixed signals on Iran — simultaneously flagging de-escalation and troop reinforcements — leave the carbon and power complex with no clear geopolitical read.
drivers: Drone attack on UAE nuclear power plant highlights expanding conflict risk to non-hydrocarbon energy infrastructure
Tata Power targets 2032 for India's first private nuclear plant as India opens civil nuclear sector
EUAs holding near monthly highs (~+3.7% 1m) despite TTF softness; Libya protests add regional power supply anxiety
